publication_scope.blurb: Louis Le Blanc de Beaulieu - Sedan Theological Theses, newly rendered from the 1675 London Latin. Covers De Theologia through Angelorum & Hominum Sanctorum Cultu Romana I-LXXVII and Pars Secunda (Reformata) I-CI, De Primi Hominis Immortalitate I-XXXV, De Justitia Primi Hominis I-LIX, De Libero Hominis Arbitrio in genere I-XLVIII, De Libero Hominis Arbitrio absolute & in se spectato (Scholae Romanae doctrina I-XLIX; Pars Tertia I-XLIII), the theses on reconciling divine concurrence with human freedom I-LIX, on human freedom and divine foreknowledge I-XLIV, and on human freedom and the divine decrees, Part One (middle knowledge) I-LXV, Part Two (the Roman doctors) I-XXXVI and Part Three (the Reformed) I-LI, and on how fallen man's free choice stands toward saving good (I-LX), and on the necessity of grace for moral good in fallen man (Pars Prior I-LIII). Not the collected folio.
publication_scope.era_note: Le Blanc wrote in the mid-seventeenth century as Reformed professor at the Academy of Sedan. This is not a patristic work. It is a public-domain Latin Reformed retrieval on the same Fathers-site pipeline. The 1675 Pitt folio is Public Domain Mark 1.0. Do not treat the site as ante-Nicene only.

source_text: XXXIII. Praesertim vero postremam hanc sententiam amplectuntur Jansenius & ejus Discipuli. Sentiunt enim omnes illi ad bonum opus morale necessariam esse gratiam, non quamlibet, sed quae sit ordinis supernaturalis, & per quam primo creatur in hominibus fides; neque haec qualiscunque, sed Christiana & infusa, quam ex pio affectu, Deo in verbo suo loquenti adhibemus. Ab ejusmodi fide incipere volunt omnem bonam volitionem, sine qua impossibile est esse aliquod bonum opus. Adeo ut opera omnia, non tantum Gentilium, sed omnium qui fide in Christum destituti sunt, quales sunt haeretici, vera & mera peccata sint, utcunque hominibus laudabilia & bona appareant.
english: It is above all Jansenius and his disciples who embrace this last view. They all hold that grace is needed for a morally good work, and not just any grace: it must be grace of the supernatural order, through which faith is first created in men. Nor is it faith of any sort, but Christian and infused faith, which out of devout affection we give to God speaking in his word.

They will have every good volition begin from faith of this kind, without which no good work can exist. So all the works not only of Gentiles but of everyone who lacks faith in Christ, such as heretics, are true and mere sins, however praiseworthy and good they look to men.

source_text: XXXIV. Hanc doctrinam ut Augustini tradit, & accurate exponit Jansenius Episcopus Iprensis in volumine quod inscripsit, Augustinus, De statu naturae lapsae libro tertio. Ibi enim capite decimo quarto pertendit, sensisse Augustinum ac ejus discipulos, & consequenter Ecclesiam Catholicam, quae doctrinam eorum in hac parte adversus Pelagianos amplexa fuit, arbitrium post lapsum hominis ita captivum esse, & boni faciendi libertate spoliatum, ut quicquid fecerit ante gratiam, hoc est, ante fidem, unde libertas a peccato incipit, non tantum nihil ad pietatem & salutem conferat, sed neque sit moraliter bonum, utpote quod sit verum & proprie dictum peccatum. Et ibidem hanc ut indubitatam Augustini & discipulorum ejus sententiam proponit, nullum, videlicet, opus bonum, ne quidem moraliter, ab humano arbitrio fieri posse, nisi per gratiam, non quamlibet, sed fidei liberetur: ut proinde ante fidem non sit ei liberum, a peccato, dum hic & nunc agere meditatur, abstinere, sed quocunque se verterit, quadam humanis viribus insolubili peccandi necessitate teneatur. Adeoque per Adami lapsum sic in homine periisse libertatem ad bonum, ut non solum non possit ante gratiam, totam justitiae moralis legem implere; sed nec quidem unum opus ejus: & ita periisse libertatem abstinendi a peccato, ut nec in uno quidem opere peccati culpam possit effugere: ac proinde inductam esse peccandi necessitatem, non tantum in aliquibus, sed in omnibus actibus. Ante gratiam enim non solum hominem non posse sine omni peccato vivere, eo quod necessario aliquando cadat; sed omnem ejus actum, antequam credat, peccatum esse, sive peccati tentationem fugere, sive amplecti videatur.
english: Jansenius, bishop of Ypres, hands this doctrine down as Augustine's and sets it out carefully in the volume he entitled Augustinus, in book 3 of On the state of fallen nature. In chapter 14 there he contends that this was the view of Augustine and his disciples, and so of the Catholic Church, which took up their teaching on this point against the Pelagians: after the fall man's choice is so captive and so stripped of the freedom to do good that whatever it does before grace, that is, before faith, from which freedom from sin begins, not only contributes nothing to piety and salvation but is not even morally good, since it is a true sin, properly so called.

In the same place he sets out as the undoubted view of Augustine and his disciples that no work that is good, even morally, can be done by human choice unless it is set free by grace, and not by any grace but by the grace of faith. Before faith, then, choice is not free to abstain from sin when it is thinking of acting here and now; whichever way it turns, it is held by a necessity of sinning that human strength cannot undo.

So, on this view, through Adam's fall man's freedom for good perished in such a way that before grace he cannot fulfil the whole law of moral righteousness, nor even one work of it. And his freedom to abstain from sin perished in such a way that he cannot escape the guilt of sin even in a single work. A necessity of sinning was therefore brought in, not in some acts only but in all.

For before grace, he holds, man not only cannot live wholly without sin, in that he necessarily falls at some time, but every act of his before he believes is a sin, whether he seems to flee the temptation to sin or to embrace it.

source_text: XXXV. Capite vero primo libri sequentis ex professo & speciatim probare aggreditur, juxta Augustinum & veritatem ipsam, omnia opera facta ante fidem, a qua religio Christiana incipit, non aliud quam peccata esse, & falso ac per errorem ipsis tribui bonitatem moralem. Et quod inde consequens est, capite octavo ostendit Philosophorum virtutes non fuisse veras virtutes, sed vitia.
english: In chapter 1 of the next book he sets out to prove, expressly and specifically, following Augustine and the truth itself, that all works done before faith, from which the Christian religion begins, are nothing but sins, and that moral goodness is ascribed to them falsely and in error.
And, as follows from this, in chapter 8 he shows that the virtues of the philosophers were not true virtues but vices.

source_text: XXXVI. Nec ad hoc ut quis bene moraliter operari possit, sufficere censet fidem inertem atque otiosam, sed requiri putat fidem actuosam, & quae sit aliquo modo per dilectionem operans. Non existimat enim ullum opus esse moraliter bonum, & effugere rationem peccati, quod non ex amore Dei & coelesti quadam charitate procedit. Illud praesertim videre est capite decimo sexto libri tertii jam citati, De statu naturae lapsae. Ubi ex Augustino docere aggreditur nullum opus bonum, hoc est, sine peccato, fieri ab homine posse, nisi ipsum benefactum diligatur: id est, nisi ipsa justitia praecepti delectet animum. Ipsa vero praecepti justitia delectari, ipsi non est aliud, quam opus bonum ex coelesti charitate prosequi: quoniam Deus justitia est, nec illa, nisi sola charitate diligitur. Et sic justitiam legis diligendo benefacere, non est aliud quam Deum ipsum charitate Spiritus Sancti diligendo, benefacere: quia Deus est ipsa justitia & veritas. Adeoque verbis ipsis Augustini affirmat nullum esse fructum bonum, qui de charitatis radice non surgit. Et tum demum, ac non aliter, aliquem incipere justitia legis delectari, quum adest fides quae per dilectionem operatur. Capite vero decimo sexto libri sequentis, ideo fidem ad bonum opus necessariam esse docet, quia ipsa est quae auxilium ad Deum amandum impetrat. Ibidemque affirmat nullum bonum opus, & nullam bonam voluntatem esse, nisi ex intentione fidei bonae, id est, ejus quae per dilectionem operatur.
english: Nor does he think an inert and idle faith is enough for someone to be able to act morally well. He holds that an active faith is required, one that in some way works through love. For he does not think any work is morally good, or escapes the character of sin, unless it proceeds from the love of God and from a kind of heavenly charity.

This is seen especially in chapter 16 of the third book already cited, On the state of fallen nature. There he sets out to teach from Augustine that no good work, that is, no work without sin, can be done by man unless the good deed itself is loved: that is, unless the righteousness of the precept itself delights the mind. For him, to delight in the righteousness of the precept is nothing other than to pursue a good work out of heavenly charity, since God is righteousness, and righteousness is loved by charity alone. So to do good by loving the righteousness of the law is nothing other than to do good by loving God himself with the charity of the Holy Spirit, because God is righteousness itself and truth.

So, in Augustine's own words, he affirms that there is no good fruit that does not spring from the root of charity, and that only then, and not otherwise, does anyone begin to delight in the righteousness of the law, when the faith that works through love is present. In chapter 16 of the next book he teaches that faith is needed for a good work because it is faith that obtains the help to love God. There too he affirms that there is no good work and no good will except from the intention of a good faith, that is, of the faith that works through love.

source_text: XXXVII. Atque ut omne bonum opus, juxta ipsum, ex sincero Dei amore procedere debet, ita quoque illud ad Deum ut finem referri necesse est. Quantumcunque vero quod aliquis agit sit, secundum substantiam, bonum, nisi faciat illud propter Deum & Dei respectu, in eo peccatum vitare non potest. Illud probare contendit capite decimo septimo libri tertii saepius allegati de statu naturae lapsae, ubi ejus pronunciatum est, Nullum omnino fieri posse opus bonum, hoc est, sine peccato, nisi ad finem in quem referri vera sapientia praecipit, hoc est in Deum propter se dilectum, referatur: alioquin nec recte fieri, neque bonum opus esse, sed veri peccati contaminatione pollutum. Unde quoque in eo libro & sequenti passim arcessit fidei necessitatem ad bene operandum, quoniam ipsa est quae ad finem illum intentionem in agendo dirigit.
english: And as on his view every good work must proceed from a sincere love of God, so too it must be referred to God as its end. However good what someone does may be in its substance, unless he does it for God and with regard to God, he cannot avoid sin in it.

He sets out to prove this in chapter 17 of the third book of On the state of fallen nature, often cited, where his thesis is: 'No good work at all, that is, no work without sin, can be done unless it is referred to the end to which true wisdom commands that it be referred, that is, to God loved for his own sake. Otherwise it is neither done rightly nor a good work, but is polluted by the contamination of true sin.'
Hence also in that book and the next he everywhere draws the necessity of faith for acting well from this: faith is what directs the intention in acting toward that end.

source_text: XXXVIII. Itaque minime probat quod plerique Scholae Romanae Theologi pro certo sumunt & statuunt, nempe ad bonum opus morale satis esse, ut procedat ex affectu naturali non malo, & ut qui agit malum finem non intendat, etiamsi de Deo non cogitet, imo nec unius veri Dei notitiam & fidem habeat. Ut quum quis, de numero eorum qui Deum ignorant, aliqua naturali compassione motus indigenti subvenit, aut parentibus honorem exhibet, & amico mutuum vel depositum reddit, quia id aequum & justum, ac rationi congruum judicat: nec tamen illud habitu, vel actu ad Dei gloriam refert, sed in sola actionis honestate acquiescit, virtutem non propter aliud, sed propter se expetens.
english: So he does not at all approve what most theologians of the Roman School take as certain and lay down: that for a morally good work it is enough that it proceed from a natural affection that is not bad, and that the agent does not intend a bad end, even if he does not think of God, and indeed does not even have knowledge of and faith in the one true God.

As when someone among those who do not know God is moved by some natural compassion to help a person in need, or honours his parents, and returns a loan or a deposit to a friend, because he judges it fair and just and in keeping with reason. Yet he does not refer it to God's glory, either habitually or actually, but rests in the mere honesty of the action, seeking virtue for its own sake and not for anything else.

source_text: XXXIX. Etenim non putat ullum esse affectum non malum qui ex sincero & casto Dei amore non profluat. Omnem enim hominis affectum, vel ad charitatem & dilectionem Dei, vel ad concupiscentiam & cupiditatem pravam pertinere; nec quicquam esse inter duo ista medium. Cum prorsus necesse sit, ut omnis noster affectus & amor, vel ad Deum tendat, & tandem in Deo terminetur; vel terminetur & sistat se in creatura aliqua, qualiscunque tandem ea supponatur: si autem sit de priori genere, illum ad charitatem spectare, & proinde bonum esse: si vero de posteriori, ad cupiditatem, & proinde malum.
english: For he does not think there is any affection that is not bad if it does not flow from a sincere and chaste love of God. Every affection of man, he holds, belongs either to charity and the love of God or to concupiscence and depraved cupidity, and there is nothing in between.

For it is absolutely necessary that all our affection and love either tend toward God and finally end in God, or end and come to rest in some creature, whatever that creature is supposed to be. If it is of the first kind, it belongs to charity and so is good; if of the second, it belongs to cupidity and so is bad.

source_text: XL. Id praesertim videre est libri illius tertii de statu naturae lapsae saepius jam citati capite decimo nono. Cujus titulus est, Non datur medium inter charitatem & culpabilem cupiditatem. Ubi istud probat ex eo quod nullum est medium inter amorem Dei, amoremque creaturae. Omnes enim, inquit, affectus animi in alicujus rei amore velut cardine versantur: qui cum non possit esse alius, nisi vel Creatoris, vel creaturae, & ille bonus hic culpabilis sit, utpote amor mundi ab Apostolo vocatus, & juxta Augustinum, ipsa ratio peccati, quae in omni malefaciendi genere dominatur: profecto liquet omnem amorem praeter istam charitatem esse culpabilem illam cupiditatem.
english: This is seen especially in chapter 19 of that third book of On the state of fallen nature, already cited often. Its title is 'There is no middle between charity and blameworthy cupidity'. There he proves it from the fact that there is no middle between the love of God and the love of the creature.

'All the affections of the mind,' he says, 'turn on the love of some thing as on a hinge. That love can only be love of the Creator or love of the creature. The first is good; the second is blameworthy, since the Apostle calls it love of the world and, according to Augustine, it is the very character of sin, which rules in every kind of wrongdoing. So it is surely clear that every love other than that charity is that blameworthy cupidity.'

source_text: XLI. Et capite praecedenti prolixe probat vitiosum esse omnem amorem mundi & creaturae, quum scilicet, creatura quaevis amatur propter se & non propter Deum. Unde colligit omnia opera, quae non referuntur ad Deum in aeterna vita possidendum, hoc ipso mala esse, quod in iis homines mundum, non Deum, diligunt: adeoque creaturae serviunt non Creatori, & concupiscentiae, seu cupiditati obediunt, quam Diabolus in homine plantavit, non charitati, quam Deus. Nec enim, inquit, inter Creatorem & creaturam, inter mundum & Deum, aliquid medium fingi potest, quod operando sectentur: vel inter cupiditatem & charitatem medius modus, quo in suis actionibus moraliter bonis impellantur. Creaturae vero cupiditate servire, potius quam Creatori, mundum inter operandum diligere, non Deum, solus impius negaverit esse peccatum. In operibus igitur illis, quantumcunque bona, & Philosophica, & sine peccato facta videantur, si sine Dei fide fiant, non sinitur dubitare Christianus, eos qui fide intentionem dirigente carent, servire creaturae, non Creatori: impossibile est enim quin alicui operando serviant. Illi quippe servit homo quod ut finem operis sui intuetur, ac diligit, sive sit ipsum opus ejus, sive objectum operis, sive (quod perpetuum est, nec excludit illa duo praecedentia) ipsemet qui opus moraliter bonum videtur operari. Hoc ipso enim quo vel vanum illum splendorem operis, ut Stoici, vel honorem, vel divitias, vel voluptatem, vel curiositatem suam operando spectat, ut alii Philosophi spectaverunt, sibi utique quicquid ut ultimum spectat appetit, non vero Deo, quem penitus nescit: atque ita nulla tergiversatione excusari potest, quin creaturae in ipso opere serviat, non Creatori.
english: In the previous chapter he proves at length that all love of the world and of the creature is vicious, that is, when any creature is loved for its own sake and not for God. From this he gathers that all works not referred to God, to be possessed in eternal life, are bad by the very fact that in them men love the world, not God. So they serve the creature, not the Creator, and obey concupiscence, or cupidity, which the devil planted in man, not charity, which God planted.

'For,' he says, 'no middle can be imagined between the Creator and the creature, between the world and God, for them to pursue in acting; nor any middle way between cupidity and charity by which they are moved in their morally good actions. Only an ungodly man would deny that it is a sin to serve the creature by cupidity rather than the Creator, and to love the world rather than God while acting.

So in those works, however good and philosophical, and however free of sin they may seem, if they are done without faith in God, a Christian may not doubt that those who lack the faith that directs the intention serve the creature, not the Creator; for it is impossible that in acting they serve no one. A man serves whatever he looks to and loves as the end of his work, whether that is his work itself, or the object of the work, or (which is always so, and does not exclude the other two) the very man who seems to be doing a morally good work.

For by the very fact that in acting he looks either to the empty splendour of the work, as the Stoics did, or to honour, riches, pleasure or his own curiosity, as other philosophers did, he seeks for himself whatever he regards as final, not for God, whom he does not know at all. So no evasion can excuse him: in that very work he serves the creature, not the Creator.'

source_text: XLII. Proinde, juxta ipsum, maxime vitiosum est ipsam virtutem propter se expetere, & virtutis officiis fungi propter solam honestatem atque pulchritudinem, qua se menti nostrae probant & commendant. Qui enim non altius assurgit, nec in eo intendit Deo servire & illi se probare, propriam excellentiam pro summo fine habet, sibique uni, qui creatura est, servire & placere cogitat, quae proculdubio summa superbia est, & maxima a vero fine deviatio, adeoque peccatum coram Deo gravissimum, quantumcunque tales actiones in oculis hominum splendeant. Nec quicquam eo excusari possunt qui virtutem ea ratione sectantur, quod virtus natura sua ad Deum referri possit, licet eo non spectet qui ex virtute agere videtur: cum caetera omnia humanae vitae bona, quae non nisi vitiose propter se expetuntur, ad Deum quoque in se spectata referri possint.
english: So on his view it is a very great vice to seek virtue itself for its own sake and to perform the duties of virtue only for the honesty and beauty by which they win our mind's approval and commend themselves to it.

For whoever rises no higher, and does not aim in this at serving God and proving himself to him, holds his own excellence as his highest end and thinks of serving and pleasing himself alone, who is a creature. That is beyond doubt the height of pride and the greatest departure from the true end, and so a very grave sin before God, however much such actions shine in men's eyes.

Those who pursue virtue in this way cannot be excused at all on the ground that virtue by its nature can be referred to God, even though the one who seems to act from virtue does not look to that. For all the other goods of human life, which are never sought for their own sake except viciously, can also be referred to God when considered in themselves.

source_text: XLIII. Quae vir ille doctus prolixe edisserit libro quarto de statu naturae lapsae capite undecimo, & aliquot sequentibus. Hoc ergo, inquit, proprium Philosophicae virtutis, quando erat etiam defaecatissima, fuit malum, quod virtutis quadam celsitudine ruinosa delectati, illam ideo expeterent, ut in oculis suis excellerent, sese oblectarent, sibi placerent, qui per illam Deo, seu, ut Augustinus loquitur, veritati placere debuissent. Quod sibi placendi malum ita arcte adhaeret iis, qui neque Deo, neque hominibus placere desiderant, ut fieri omnino non possit, quin in illud incidant. Nam ut paulo post subjungit, Qui non levat oculos suos ad Deum, ut ei de pulchritudine virtutis placeat, sed ipsam unice, velut finem boni, pulcherrimam celsissimamque miratur, impossibile est, ut eam vel appetens non inde sibi placeat, vel non inde sibi placere volens appetat. Cum enim necessarium omnino sit, ut aliqua re mens humana delectetur, quo quaeso alio oblectari potest mens aliena a Deo, caeterasque viliores contemnens creaturas, ut supponimus, quam illo quod in rebus creatis praestantissimum credit? Hoc est autem mens ipsa virtute jam decorata, quem sui ipsius ornatum omnium pulcherrimum arbitratur. Sibi ipsi ergo necessario de virtute placet, qui per eam Deo, vel aliis hominibus placere non cupit. Unde concludit, sola voluntate placendi per virtutem Deo, evitari posse, ne virtus non modo Gentilium Philosophica, sed & Christiana sibi ipsi superbiendo placeat, & vitium, quae virtus esse putabatur, fiat.
english: That learned man discusses this at length in book 4 of On the state of fallen nature, chapter 11 and several chapters after it. 'This, then,' he says, 'was the evil proper to the philosophers' virtue, even when it was at its most refined: delighted by a kind of ruinous loftiness of virtue, they sought it so that they might excel in their own eyes, take delight in themselves and please themselves, when through it they ought to have pleased God, or, as Augustine puts it, the truth. This evil of self-pleasing clings so closely to those who desire to please neither God nor men that they cannot possibly avoid falling into it.'

For, as he adds a little later, 'Whoever does not lift his eyes to God, to please him by the beauty of virtue, but admires virtue alone as the end of good, most beautiful and most lofty, cannot seek it without pleasing himself by it, nor seek it without wishing to please himself by it. Since the human mind must take delight in something, in what else, I ask, can a mind estranged from God, which looks down on the other, lower creatures, as we are supposing, take delight than in what it believes most excellent among created things? That is the mind itself, now adorned with virtue, an adornment of its own that it judges the most beautiful of all. So whoever does not desire through virtue to please God or other men necessarily pleases himself by his virtue.'

From this he concludes that only by the will to please God through virtue can it be avoided that virtue, not only the philosophical virtue of the Gentiles but Christian virtue too, should please itself through pride and become a vice, which had been thought to be a virtue.

source_text: XLIV. Porro cum, ex Jansenii mente, nullum sit bonum opus quod non ex coelesti quadam charitate profluat, atque ad Deum in aeterna vita possidendum non referatur, inde quoque consequens est, nullum esse bonum opus, quod non ad Dei cultum & pietatem pertineat, & suo modo prosit ad animae salutem. Adeoque frustra Scholasticos distinguere bona opera in ea quae solum moraliter bona sunt, nec possunt inter actus pietatis & religionis censeri; ac proinde facienti nihil prosunt ad vitam aeternam: & ea in quibus pietas & religio consistit, & quae sic ad salutem animae & vitam aeternam aliquid conferunt.
english: Further, since in Jansenius's mind there is no good work that does not flow from a kind of heavenly charity and is not referred to God, to be possessed in eternal life, it also follows that there is no good work that does not belong to the worship of God and to piety and in its own way profit the soul's salvation.

So the Schoolmen divide good works in vain into those that are only morally good, cannot be counted among acts of piety and religion, and so profit the doer nothing toward eternal life, and those in which piety and religion consist and which in this way contribute something to the soul's salvation and eternal life.

source_text: XLV. Quod corollarium Jansenius ipse ex doctrina sua educit, de statu Naturae lapsae libro quarto capite secundo, ubi haec sunt illius verba, Fieri enim nullo pacto potest ut opus quod ex fide & amore Dei nascitur, non etiam hoc ipso sit opus pietatis, justitiae, cultus Dei, meritorium, beatificum. Quae namque praeclarior pietas, & justitia, & cultus Dei, quam Dei amor ex fide? Quid magis meritorium atque beatificum, id est, ad beatitudinem aliquid conferens, quam Dei amor ex fide? Et postea, se sentire cum Augustino declarat, quod nullum omnino sit, vel esse possit bonum opus, quin hoc ipso, sicut fidem amoremque Dei, velut sui principium, postulat; ita sit etiam pietatis & cultus Dei, aeternaeque vitae suo modo meritorium. Et cap. decimo quinto reprehendens divisionem virtutum & affectuum, qua utebatur olim Julianus Pelagianus, dicendo quosdam esse per quos sumus steriliter boni; alios vero per quos fructuose boni sumus, id est, qui ad vitam aeternam consequendam, ut docent Scholastici, aut prosunt, aut non prosunt, Cum enim, inquit, nulla virtus aut sit, aut esse possit, quae non faciat opus ex fide atque dilectione veri Dei, ad quem omne opus virtutis referri debet; & si non referatur, ipso non recto fine, peccatum est: impossibile est virtutem ullam esse sterilem. Fides enim & amor Dei sterilis esse nullo modo potest: sed si sterilis est, non jam virtus, sed vitium esse debet.
english: Jansenius himself draws this corollary from his doctrine in book 4 of On the state of fallen nature, chapter 2, where his words are: 'It is in no way possible that a work born of faith and the love of God should not by that very fact also be a work of piety, of righteousness, of the worship of God, meritorious and beatific. For what piety, righteousness and worship of God is more excellent than the love of God from faith? What is more meritorious and beatific, that is, more conducive to blessedness, than the love of God from faith?'

Later he declares that he holds with Augustine that there neither is nor can be any good work which, just as it requires faith and the love of God as its principle, is not by that very fact also a work of piety and of the worship of God and in its own way meritorious of eternal life.

In chapter 15 he criticizes the division of virtues and affections that Julian the Pelagian once used, saying that there are some through which we are good barrenly and others through which we are good fruitfully, that is, those which, as the Schoolmen teach, either help toward obtaining eternal life or do not. 'Since there neither is nor can be any virtue,' he says, 'that does not do its work from faith and love of the true God, to whom every work of virtue must be referred, and if it is not so referred it is a sin by the very fact that its end is not right, no virtue can possibly be barren. For faith and the love of God can in no way be barren; if it is barren, it is no longer virtue but must be vice.'

source_text: XLVI. Quamvis autem vir ille nullum bonum opus agnoscat, nisi quod a charitate & fide quodammodo per dilectionem operante procedat, non negat tamen peccatores, hoc est, in peccato mortali constitutos, & qui nondum justificati sunt, & peccatorum suorum remissionem adepti, posse quaedam bona opera facere. Atque in eo subscribit Tridentinae Synodo, quae anathema dicit iis qui affirmant omnia opera quae ante justificationem fiunt, vera esse peccata. Si quis dixerit, inquit, Opera omnia quae ante justificationem fiunt, quacunque ratione facta sint, vera esse peccata, vel odium Dei mereri, anathema sit. Canone septimo Sessionis sextae.
english: Although that man acknowledges no good work except what proceeds from charity and from faith working in some way through love, he does not deny that sinners, that is, those in mortal sin, who have not yet been justified and obtained the forgiveness of their sins, can do some good works.

In this he subscribes to the Council of Trent, which pronounces anathema on those who affirm that all works done before justification are true sins: 'If anyone says that all works done before justification, in whatever way they are done, are true sins or merit God's hatred, let him be anathema.' Session 6, canon 7.

source_text: XLVII. Istud videre est apud Jansenium De statu naturae lapsae libro quarto capite quarto. Nam, inquit, quamvis verissimum sit opera peccatorum omnium, imo etiam justorum, quae non referuntur ad eum finem ad quem referri debent, hoc est, ad Deum, sed in creaturis haerent, vera esse peccata: falsum est tamen eandem de peccatoribus fidelibus, quam infidelibus esse rationem. Hoc ipso enim quo peccatores fide imbuti sunt, quanquam perfecta illa charitate Deum super omnia diligente, hoc est, justificatione, destituti sint, multa tamen bona ex illa fide operari possunt; sicut in primis ipsum credere & operari velle, & si adhuc viribus careant, infirmitatem suam ingemiscere, ex fide justificationem, vel operandi vires impetrare, cujusmodi opera Augustinus semper peccatoribus tribuit. Et postea probare volens fideles quantislibet peccatis mancipatos non carere imperfecto quodam amore Dei, qui sincerus tamen sit & verae pietatis initium, quali Dei amore carent prorsus infideles, Hoc ipso, inquit, quo adhuc fideles permanent, non possunt non habere affectum illum verae pietatis atque dilectionis, ex quo credunt Deo, ex quo sperant subinde beatitudinem, ex quo orant pro impetranda perfecta charitate, atque justitia; ex quo etiam alia nonnulla bona sincero Dei intuitu operantur, quamvis necdum ita diligant, ut eum omnibus terrenis amoribus, ac delectationibus praeferant.
english: This is seen in Jansenius, On the state of fallen nature, book 4, chapter 4. 'Although it is most true,' he says, 'that the works of all sinners, and even of the righteous, which are not referred to the end to which they ought to be referred, that is, to God, but stick fast in creatures, are true sins, it is false that the case is the same for believing sinners as for unbelievers.

For by the very fact that sinners are imbued with faith, even though they lack that perfect charity which loves God above all, that is, justification, they can still do many good things from that faith: first of all, believing itself and willing to act, and, if they still lack the strength, groaning over their weakness and obtaining from faith justification or the strength to act. Augustine always ascribes works of this kind to sinners.'

Later, wishing to prove that believers, however enslaved to sins, do not lack a certain imperfect love of God, which is nonetheless sincere and the beginning of true piety, a love of God that unbelievers wholly lack, he says: 'By the very fact that they still remain believers they cannot fail to have that affection of true piety and love from which they believe God, from which they hope for blessedness in due course, from which they pray to obtain perfect charity and righteousness, and from which they also do some other good things with a sincere regard to God, although they do not yet love him so as to prefer him to all earthly loves and delights.'

source_text: XLVIII. Distinguit enim ille inter charitatem proprie dictam, qua Deus super omnia diligitur: & inter charitatem quandam imperfectam, qua Deus gratis quidem & propter se, non tamen super omnia diligitur. Ex ejus mente, prior illa charitas est ipsa justitia nostra; nec reperiri potest, nisi in justificatis, ac proinde non amplius in peccato haerentibus. Posterior vero reperiri potest etiam in peccatoribus, necdum per Dei gratiam a peccatorum suorum reatu liberatis: in quibus per auxilia a Christo subministrata, excitantur quidam actus fidei & dilectionis, per quos peccatores ad recipiendam a Deo justitiam, & peccatorum suorum remissionem disponuntur.
english: For he distinguishes charity properly so called, by which God is loved above all, from a certain imperfect charity, by which God is loved freely indeed and for his own sake, yet not above all.

In his mind the first charity is our very righteousness and can be found only in the justified, and so in those no longer stuck in sin. The second can be found even in sinners not yet freed by God's grace from the guilt of their sins. In them, through helps supplied by Christ, certain acts of faith and love are stirred up, by which sinners are disposed to receive righteousness from God and the forgiveness of their sins.

source_text: XLIX. Et tamen, juxta ipsum, amor ille imperfectus non est solum, ut opinantur recentiores nonnulli Scholastici, amor quidam Dei implicitus, & in intentione alicujus honestatis moralis involutus, sed verus & formalis aliquis Dei amor; sine quo amore creatoris nullus, secundum Augustinum, bene utitur creaturis, sive fidelis, sive infidelis, sive justus, sive peccator sit: & quo fidelis, etiam peccator, in quibusdam operibus nequaquam caret. Adeoque ex viri illius sententia, charitas seu amor de quo jam quaestio est, & quo fideles, quamvis in peccato jacentes, non omnino destituuntur, est imperfecta Dei dilectio, seu imperfecta quaedam in Deo complacentia, quae charitatem illam vulgo notam, & Deum super omnia diligentem praevolat, & omnem inchoat justitiam. Ut latius videre est apud authorem istum, cap. illo 4. lib. 4. de statu naturae lapsae.
english: Yet on his view that imperfect love is not merely, as some more recent Schoolmen think, an implicit love of God wrapped up in the intention of some moral honesty. It is a true and formal love of God; without this love of the Creator no one, according to Augustine, uses creatures well, whether he is a believer or an unbeliever, righteous or a sinner; and a believer, even a sinner, by no means lacks it in certain works.

So in that man's view the charity, or love, now in question, which believers do not wholly lack even when lying in sin, is an imperfect love of God, or a certain imperfect delight in God. It goes before the charity commonly known, the charity that loves God above all, and it begins all righteousness. This can be seen more fully in that author, in that chapter 4 of book 4 of On the state of fallen nature.

source_text: L. Caeterum quamvis non pauci Scholae Romanae Theologi nullum bonum opus morale sine gratia Christi perfici posse existiment, ac censeant plerique illius Scholae Doctores difficiliora saltem legis moralis praecepta sine gratiae illius auxilio servari non posse: imo ne uni quidem ex facilioribus, nisi auxiliante Christo, obsequium praestari posse, si gravis aliqua tentatio urgeat; in eo tamen omnes conveniunt hominem, etiam in statu naturae lapsae, circa res morales libertatem habere, liberique arbitrii esse, & dici debere, non solum in rebus civilibus atque naturalibus, sed etiam in moralibus.
english: Not a few theologians of the Roman School think that no morally good work can be accomplished without the grace of Christ. Most doctors of that School hold that at least the harder precepts of the moral law cannot be kept without the help of that grace, and that not even one of the easier ones can be obeyed without Christ's help if some heavy temptation presses.

Yet in this they all agree: man, even in the state of fallen nature, has freedom in moral matters; he has free choice and ought to be said to have it, not only in civil and natural matters but in moral ones too.

source_text: LI. Istud videre est apud Bellarminum. Controversia est, inquit, inter Catholicos omnes ab una parte, & Hereticos omnes hujus temporis (neque enim hac in re vel apud nostros, vel apud adversarios ulla est opinionum varietas) sitne homo in statu naturae lapsae liberi arbitrii in bono morali eligendo, & malo evitando, sive quod idem est in praeceptis morum observandis, aut praevaricandis. Et quidem Catholici omnes, tum veteres tum recentiores, tanquam dogma fidei Catholicae praedicant partem affirmantem. De libero Arbitrio lib. 5. cap. 13.
english: This is seen in Bellarmine. 'The controversy,' he says, 'is between all Catholics on one side and all the heretics of this time on the other (for on this point there is no variety of opinion either among our own or among our adversaries): whether man in the state of fallen nature has free choice in choosing moral good and avoiding evil, or, what is the same, in keeping or breaking the precepts of morals.
And all Catholics, both the old and the more recent, proclaim the affirmative as a dogma of the Catholic faith.' On free choice, book 5, chapter 13.

source_text: LII. Itaque apud eos Dogma Catholicum est, hominem etiam peccato corruptum, quum bene moraliter agit, libertate sua uti: nec eum minus libere legis moralis praecepta transgredi, vel committendo quae vetant, vel omittendo quae jubent: sive ad bene moraliter agendum gratia necessaria supponatur, sive non. Quae quaestio ab hac diversa est, & super qua, ut vidimus, Doctores Scholae Romanae non eodem modo opinantur: cum tamen nullus inter eos neget, hominem lapsum circa bonum morale liberum suum arbitrium habere.
english: So among them it is Catholic dogma that man, even when corrupted by sin, uses his freedom when he acts morally well, and transgresses the precepts of the moral law no less freely, whether by doing what they forbid or by leaving undone what they command, whether or not grace is supposed necessary for acting morally well.

That is a different question from this one, and on it, as we have seen, the doctors of the Roman School are not of one opinion; yet none of them denies that fallen man has his free choice with regard to moral good.

source_text: LIII. Sic quaestionis hujus sensum exponit ipse Bellarminus, Non enim, inquit, disputamus hoc loco, possitne lex solis naturae viribus adimpleri, nec ignoramus auxilium gratiae esse modis omnibus necessarium, cum lex sola non faciat justos, sed contra potius per gratiam justificati faciant legem. Sed quaestio nostra est, utrum posito auxilio gratiae, homo sit vere liberi arbitrii, ita ut possit legem implere, vel eandem, si maluerit, praevaricari. Quomodo si quis quaerat, An possit homo pro arbitrio videre, & non videre; non oportet objicere, quid si lumen absit? intelligitur enim quaestio positis omnibus quae necessario requiruntur. Nos igitur dicimus, posito auxilio necessario, quodcunque illud sit, hominem vere proprieque liberum esse in moralibus. De Gratia & libero arbitrio libro quinto cap. 18.
english: Bellarmine himself explains the sense of this question as follows. 'We are not disputing here,' he says, 'whether the law can be fulfilled by the strength of nature alone. Nor are we unaware that the help of grace is in every way necessary, since the law alone does not make men righteous; rather, those justified through grace do the law.

Our question is whether, once the help of grace is supposed, man truly has free choice, so that he can fulfil the law or, if he prefers, transgress it. Just as, if someone asks whether a man can see or not see at will, one should not object, "What if there is no light?", for the question is understood with everything supposed that is necessarily required.
We say, then, that once the necessary help is supposed, whatever it may be, man is truly and properly free in moral matters.' On grace and free choice, book 5, chapter 18.
